title: Rethinking Visual Reasoning in Text-to-Image Reward Modeling
claim: Existing models trade off understanding for preference accuracy; mixing in a new pairing type improves both and yields better outputs.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, each with gray caption bar forming a narrative
description: Three framed panels, each with a gray caption bar at the bottom that reads as a left-to-right story. The left panel is a scatter plot of visual reasoning accuracy against preference pairs accuracy. Baselines (Qwen, CLIP, ImageReward, HPSv2, HPSv3, PickScore) are black triangles with white labels. A red dashed arrow runs from the strong VLM backbones down to HPSv3 and is annotated 'Learn preferences, forget visual reasoning!'. A red star labeled 'Ours' sits at the upper right. The center panel has a gray box for standard pairs, two cyberpunk city images labeled Pref and Dispref. A plus sign leads to a green box for CrossPairs, with one photo of a person and a zebra and two contrasting prompts, 'in front of' versus 'behind'. The right panel shows two generated images of a hilltop building, before and after, joined by a green arrow. Black arrows link bolded prompt words to the image details.
caption: (Left) Existing reward models exhibit poor visual understanding. VLM backbones possess strong visual reasoning, but this is eroded during preference fine-tuning, even with robust fine-tuning techniques. (Center) We introduce CrossPairs -- preference pairs sharing a common image but differing in prompt -- to isolate text-image alignment signal by eliminating aesthetic confounds. Mixed with standard pairs during training, our method achieves a Pareto improvement. (Right) The resulting reward model guides generations with superior compositional accuracy.
abstract: Reward models are a core component of modern text-to-image systems, serving as the objective for inference-time selection and RL-based post-training. A key prerequisite is visual understanding: to judge prompt adherence and ground aesthetic preferences, a reward model must bind attributes, resolve relations, and count reliably. We find that widely-used reward models perform poorly on targeted visual reasoning evaluations. Even when starting from strong vision-language backbones, preference fine-tuning erodes these capabilities, and continual-learning baselines fail to mitigate a steep tradeoff between visual reasoning and preference accuracy. We propose a data-centric intervention that injects visual reasoning supervision into preference learning by flipping the pairing axis. To complement conventional human preference data (paired images under a shared prompt), we convert existing visual reasoning datasets into preference pairs that share the same image but differ in prompt, and train on the mixture. This yields a Pareto improvement in both visual understanding and preference prediction. Across inference-time best-of-n selection and RL post-training, the resulting reward model improves text-to-image generation on challenging compositional prompts (GenEval) by an average of 4.0% and 5.5% respectively, outperforming HPSv3 which was trained on 6x more preference pairs.
